reason: Beach shingle (rounded pebbles) is British usage. For American readers, and the edition is in American English, a ‘shingle’ is a roofing tile or a signboard, and ‘a beach of shingle’ cannot be pictured. Homer’s point is the pebbles the sea washes up (6.94–95), on which the clean laundry is spread. ‘pebbles’ is plain English on both sides of the Atlantic and adds nothing. Unlike the case for keeping ‘draughts’ (GLOSSARY), the replacement is not a regionalism. D29 would keep ‘shingle’ if the lead judges it current enough for the edition’s readers, which is why this is optional.

old: for he was in great want
new: for he was in great need
reason: ‘want’ meaning need is one of the brief’s dead senses, and here the living sense is a hazard. A naked man approaching young women ‘for he was in great want’ can be read as desire, which inverts his motive and the decorum of the scene. Homer: ‘for need had come upon him’ (6.136). ‘need’ fixes the sense with one word. The living idioms ‘for want of a foothold’ (5.30) and ‘you shall not want for clothes’ (6.14) are not affected and are kept. It is optional because most readers take ‘in want’ as need, as this reader did.

old: in the middle of it, paved with large stones
new: in the middle of it, and paved with large stones
reason: The candidate dropped Butler’s ‘and’, which leaves ‘paved with large stones’ attached to the nearest noun, the temple, so the reader had to guess which of the two is paved. In Homer the paved space is the assembly place around the temple (6.266–267). Restoring Butler’s own ‘and’ (D29) makes ‘paved’ a second predicate of the marketplace, and no other word moves.
